cards.front: What are the three classifications of investment companies under the Investment Company Act of 1940?
cards.back: 1) Face-Amount Certificate (FAC) companies, 2) Unit Investment Trusts (UITs), and 3) Management Investment Companies (open-end and closed-end).

cards.front: Face-Amount Certificate (FAC)
cards.back: A contract in which the issuer guarantees payment of a stated (face) amount to the investor at a set future date in exchange for a lump sum or periodic payments. Classified as an investment company under the 1940 Act, though few operate today.

cards.front: Unit Investment Trust (UIT)
cards.back: An investment company organized under a trust indenture with trustees (no board of directors). Sells redeemable units representing an undivided interest in a fixed, unmanaged portfolio of securities. Terminates at bond maturity or a preset date.

cards.front: How does a closed-end fund differ from an open-end fund in terms of capitalization and securities issued?
cards.back: Closed-end: fixed capitalization (one-time IPO), may issue common stock, preferred stock, and bonds, and trades in the secondary market. Open-end: unlimited capitalization (continuous offering), issues only common stock (no debt or preferred), and shares are redeemed by the fund only.

cards.front: How is the price of a closed-end fund share determined versus an open-end fund share?
cards.back: Closed-end shares trade at current market value (CMV) determined by supply and demand on an exchange or OTC — may trade at a premium or discount to NAV. Open-end (mutual fund) shares are priced by formula at NAV + sales charge (POP) using forward pricing.

cards.front: Why are FACs, UITs, and open-end funds (mutual funds) NOT traded in the secondary market?
cards.back: All three are redeemable securities — investors must redeem shares through the issuer rather than sell them to other investors in the secondary market.

cards.front: What is the maximum sales charge allowed on a mutual fund under the Investment Company Act of 1940?
cards.back: 8.5% of the public offering price (POP).

cards.front: Class A mutual fund shares
cards.back: Front-end load shares. Sales charge is deducted from the investment at the time of purchase. Best for investors with large investments (to access breakpoints) and longer time horizons. Typically have lower ongoing expenses than B or C shares.

cards.front: Class B mutual fund shares
cards.back: Back-end load shares with a Contingent Deferred Sales Charge (CDSC) that declines annually and typically reaches zero after 5–7 years, after which they convert to Class A shares. Best for smaller investments held for long periods. Higher ongoing expenses than Class A.

cards.front: Class C mutual fund shares
cards.back: Level-load shares — typically a 1% CDSC for one year, plus an ongoing 0.75% 12b-1 fee and 0.25% shareholder services fee. Best for investors with short time horizons (1–5 years) because ongoing fees never end.

cards.front: Which class of mutual fund shares qualifies for breakpoints?
cards.back: Only Class A (front-end load) shares qualify for breakpoint discounts.

cards.front: A customer wishes to invest $23,000 in a fund where breakpoints reduce the sales charge from 6.5% to 4.0% at the $25,000 level. What is the registered representative required to do?
cards.back: The RR must inform the customer that investing an additional $2,000 would qualify for the next breakpoint and reduce the sales charge to 4%. Failing to disclose this constitutes a 'breakpoint sale' violation.

cards.front: Letter of Intent (LOI)
cards.back: A one-sided agreement (binding only on the fund) in which the investor commits to invest enough additional money to reach a breakpoint within 13 months. May be backdated up to 90 days. The fund holds extra shares in escrow until the LOI is completed.

cards.front: How do rights of accumulation differ from a Letter of Intent?
cards.back: Rights of accumulation: apply to subsequent (not initial) investments, allow prior share appreciation to count toward breakpoints, and have no time limit. LOI: must be completed within 13 months, may be backdated 90 days, and appreciation/reinvested dividends do NOT count.

cards.front: A mutual fund has total assets of $100 million, liabilities of $5 million, and 10 million shares outstanding. Calculate the NAV per share.
cards.back: Net assets = $100M − $5M = $95M. NAV per share = $95M ÷ 10M shares = $9.50 per share.

cards.front: What expenses are included in a mutual fund's expense ratio?
cards.back: Manager's (investment adviser's) fee, administrative fees (transfer agents, accountants, attorneys), board of directors' costs, and 12b-1 fees. Sales charges (loads) are NOT included in the expense ratio.

cards.front: What is forward pricing for mutual fund shares?
cards.back: Purchase and redemption orders are executed at the next NAV calculated after the order is received. Funds compute NAV at least once per business day, typically at 4:00 pm ET. Orders received after the cutoff are priced at the next business day's NAV.

cards.front: What is a 'breakpoint sale' and why is it a violation?
cards.back: A breakpoint sale is soliciting a mutual fund purchase in an amount just below a breakpoint to generate a higher sales charge (and commission). It violates just and equitable principles of trade. The violation is the failure to disclose the breakpoint, not the customer's choice to invest a lower amount.

cards.front: What is the order of dividend distribution dates for a mutual fund, and who sets the ex-date?
cards.back: Declaration date → Record date / Payable date (same day) → Ex-dividend date (day AFTER record date). The mutual fund's Board of Directors sets the ex-date — not FINRA or an exchange.

cards.front: Statutory (full) prospectus
cards.back: The full and fair disclosure document containing all material information needed to make an informed investment decision: fund objective, policies, sales charges, expenses, services, and 1-, 5-, and 10-year performance history (or life of fund if shorter). Must be delivered before or during solicitation.

cards.front: Summary prospectus (Rule 498)
cards.back: A standardized short-form summary of key information from the full prospectus that may include a purchase application. Investors who buy via the summary must have access to the full prospectus no later than the trade confirmation.

cards.front: Statement of Additional Information (SAI)
cards.back: Supplemental document containing the fund's history, policies, consolidated financial statements (balance sheet, income statement, statement of operations, portfolio list). Must be available without charge within three business days of an investor's request.

cards.front: Omitting prospectus (Rule 482)
cards.back: A mutual fund advertisement (sometimes called a tombstone ad). It does not provide full and fair disclosure, so delivery of an omitting prospectus is NOT sufficient to execute a trade.

cards.front: Under Subchapter M (conduit/pipeline tax theory), what percentage of net investment income must a mutual fund distribute to avoid taxation at the fund level?
cards.back: At least 90% of net investment income (NII) must be distributed to shareholders. The fund then pays tax only on the undistributed portion. If less than 90% is distributed, the fund is taxed on 100% of NII.

cards.front: A balanced fund earned $500,000 in dividends and $600,000 in interest, with $100,000 in expenses. To qualify as a regulated investment company under Subchapter M, what is the minimum it must distribute to shareholders?
cards.back: Net Investment Income = $500,000 + $600,000 − $100,000 = $1,000,000. Minimum required distribution = 90% × $1,000,000 = $900,000. The fund will still pay tax on any NII it retains; shareholders pay tax on what they receive.

cards.front: Are reinvested mutual fund dividend and capital gains distributions taxable to the shareholder?
cards.back: Yes. Although reinvestments are made at NAV (no sales charge) and add to the investor's cost basis, all distributions — whether taken in cash or reinvested — are taxable in the year received.

cards.front: May a registered representative highlight or annotate a mutual fund prospectus to draw attention to key sections?
cards.back: No. A prospectus may never be altered in any way — no highlighting, writing in, or marking. It must be delivered exactly as published.

cards.front: Can investment clubs combine purchases to qualify for mutual fund breakpoints?
cards.back: No. Individuals, spouses, minor children, and corporations (including divisions and subsidiaries) may combine purchases to qualify for breakpoints. Investment clubs may NOT.
